Alpha-1 antitrypsin level
move.howTo: One tube. It is an acute-phase protein, so a borderline level during an infection is repeated when well.

move.label: Alpha-1 antitrypsin phenotype (Pi typing)
move.howTo: Isoelectric focusing or a genotype for S and Z. It is what turns a low level into a diagnosis and tells the family what to test for.

move.label: Morning cortisol
move.howTo: Between 8 and 9 in the morning, off any steroid including inhaled and skin preparations. Under 5 is diagnostic, over 15 excludes it.

move.label: ACTH stimulation test
move.howTo: 250 µg synthetic ACTH, cortisol at 30 and 60 minutes. A peak under 18 µg/dL confirms it. Book it through an endocrinologist.

move.label: Morning testosterone, repeated
move.howTo: Before 10 am, fasted, twice on separate days. A single afternoon sample is the commonest reason this gets diagnosed wrongly.

move.label: Repeat LDL off any treatment
Colonoscopy
move.howTo: From 45, every ten years if it is clean, and from 40 with a first-degree relative — or ten years before their diagnosis if that is earlier. A faecal immunochemical test every year is the cheaper alternative with almost as much mortality evidence.

move.label: Alpha-galactosidase A activity (dried blood spot)
move.howTo: A dried blood spot posted to a metabolic laboratory. Diagnostic in males; in females it can be normal and the GLA gene is what answers the question.

move.label: Exome sequencing
move.howTo: A blood tube and a consent conversation, reported in six to twelve weeks by a genetics service. It answers every single-gene disease at once, including the ones nobody thought of, and it is the only test on this list that can come back with something you did not ask about. Here it is on the table because Fabry disease would each be settled by it.

move.label: ApoB
move.howTo: No fast needed. It counts the particles rather than the cholesterol inside them, which is what actually enters the artery wall.

move.label: Repeat hs-CRP after 2 weeks
move.howTo: Never interpret one CRP. Repeat it two weeks after any infection has cleared; the lower of two readings is the one that means anything.

move.label: HBsAg with anti-HCV
move.howTo: Once in a lifetime for every adult, per the WHO and US CDC. Two lines on a lab form and one of the two results is curable.

move.label: 7-day home blood pressure average
move.howTo: Twice a morning and twice an evening for seven days, sitting, arm supported, after five minutes still. Throw the first day away and average the rest.

move.label: Uric acid
move.howTo: Not during an attack: urate often reads normal in the middle of one. Wait two weeks.

move.label: VO2max estimate from a submaximal test
move.howTo: A twelve-minute run, a step test or a watch estimate. Any of them beats not measuring it, which is what almost every clinic does.

move.label: Red cell folate
move.howTo: Reflects the last three months rather than last night's dinner, which is what you want when the serum is borderline.

move.label: Coronary calcium score (CAC)
move.howTo: A two-minute CT, about 1 mSv. A zero score in a 50-year-old buys years of reassurance; a high score changes the conversation about statins.

move.label: OGTT
move.howTo: Two hours after 75 g of glucose. It catches the people whose fasting numbers look fine and whose post-meal ones do not.

move.label: OGTT with insulin
move.howTo: 75 g glucose, insulin at 0 and 120 minutes. Ask for insulin, not glucose alone.

move.label: Morning testosterone, repeated
move.howTo: Before 10 am, fasted, twice on separate days. A single afternoon sample is the commonest reason this gets diagnosed wrongly.

move.label: STOP-Bang questionnaire
move.howTo: Eight yes/no questions, two minutes, free. Three or more is a positive screen.

move.label: Full AUDIT questionnaire
move.howTo: Ten questions, free, and better than any blood test. Eight or more means dependence is likely.

move.howTo: One draw, no fast needed for a modern panel. It reports total, LDL, HDL and triglycerides; the LDL is what the risk rules read, and apoB is the better follow-up when it comes back high.

move.label: Full AUDIT questionnaire
move.howTo: Ten questions, free, and better than any blood test. Eight or more means dependence is likely.

move.label: HBsAg with anti-HCV
move.howTo: Once in a lifetime for every adult, per the WHO and US CDC. Two lines on a lab form and one of the two results is curable.

move.label: VO2max estimate from a submaximal test
move.howTo: A twelve-minute run, a step test or a watch estimate. Any of them beats not measuring it, which is what almost every clinic does.

move.label: 7-day home blood pressure average
move.howTo: Twice a morning and twice an evening for seven days, sitting, arm supported, after five minutes still. Throw the first day away and average the rest.

move.label: Red cell folate
move.howTo: Reflects the last three months rather than last night's dinner, which is what you want when the serum is borderline.

move.label: STOP-Bang questionnaire
move.howTo: Eight yes/no questions, two minutes, free. Three or more is a positive screen.

move.label: Do you get coarse dark hair on your face, chest or stomach, or acne that will not settle?
Are your periods regular, irregular, heavy, or absent?
Repeat TSH in 6 months
move.howTo: Progression runs 2–5 % per year while antibody-positive, so a second TSH is the cheapest test there is.

move.label: HbA1c
move.howTo: No fast needed. It averages the last three months, so a single bad week does not move it.

move.label: Lp(a) once
move.howTo: Once in a life. Ask for the molar unit (nmol/L) if the lab offers it; mass units vary between assays.

move.label: Total and free testosterone
move.howTo: Morning draw, days 2–5 of the cycle if there is one.

move.label: Ferritin
move.howTo: Draw it with a CRP: inflammation lifts ferritin and hides an empty store.

move.label: Serum folate
move.howTo: Fasting, and before any supplement: one folic-acid tablet normalises the serum level within a day.

move.label: Haemoglobin electrophoresis
move.howTo: An HbA2 above 3.5 % is beta-thalassaemia trait. Worth knowing once, mostly so nobody prescribes you iron forever.

move.label: Repeat B12
Repeat B12
Pepsinogen I and II with gastrin-17
move.howTo: The serological biopsy: it says which part of the stomach is atrophic without an endoscope.

move.label: Repeat LDL off any treatment
Mammography
move.howTo: Every two years from 50, and from 40 by preference. With a strong family history it starts at 30, and a genetics referral is what decides whether MRI is added to it.

move.label: Haemoglobin electrophoresis
move.howTo: An HbA2 above 3.5 % is beta-thalassaemia trait. Worth knowing once, mostly so nobody prescribes you iron forever.

move.label: Red cell folate
move.howTo: Reflects the last three months rather than last night's dinner, which is what you want when the serum is borderline.

move.label: Colonoscopy
move.howTo: From 45, every ten years if it is clean, and from 40 with a first-degree relative — or ten years before their diagnosis if that is earlier. A faecal immunochemical test every year is the cheaper alternative with almost as much mortality evidence.

move.label: Thyroid ultrasound
move.howTo: 1 for a heterogeneous, hypoechoic gland, 0 for a normal one. Also baselines nodules.

move.label: What is your home blood pressure, averaged over 7 days? Write it as 120/80.
Have you ever had a sudden painful, swollen joint, usually the big toe or ankle?
Over the last 2 weeks: little interest or pleasure in doing things?
Does your abdomen bloat or distend after meals, most days?
Hydrogen and methane breath test
move.howTo: Glucose or lactulose after a preparation day, then breath samples every 15-20 minutes for two hours. A 20 ppm rise inside 90 minutes is positive.

Over the last 2 weeks: little interest or pleasure in doing things?
What is your waist, in centimetres, measured at the navel?
Do you fall asleep when you are sitting quietly during the day?
How often do you have a drink containing alcohol?
Have you been tired most days for over a month?
Is your hair thinning, or your skin very dry?
Over the last 2 weeks: feeling down, depressed or hopeless?
Does your abdomen bloat or distend after meals, most days?
Do you snore, or has anyone told you that you stop breathing at night?
Are you unusually thirsty, or urinating much more than usual?
Do you have cold hands and feet, or feel cold when others do not?
Do you get pins and needles or numbness in your hands or feet?
Do you crave salt or salty food, enough that you add it to everything or eat it straight?
Do you go dizzy or grey out when you stand up quickly, most days?
Have your hands become shaky, or your handwriting or speech changed?
Ceruloplasmin
move.howTo: One tube, no preparation. It is an acute-phase protein, so a normal value during an infection does not exclude anything.

move.label: 24-hour urine copper
move.howTo: A full day's urine in an acid-washed container. Slit-lamp for Kayser-Fleischer rings is booked at the same time.

move.label: Exome sequencing
move.howTo: A blood tube and a consent conversation, reported in six to twelve weeks by a genetics service. It answers every single-gene disease at once, including the ones nobody thought of, and it is the only test on this list that can come back with something you did not ask about. Here it is on the table because Wilson disease would each be settled by it.
